title: The American founding and the young republic
note: After declaring independence in 1776, Americans first tried a weak league of states under the Articles of Confederation, then wrote the Constitution of 1787, a federal system of separated powers, soon amended by a Bill of Rights. The young nation expanded west, while compromises over slavery postponed a reckoning.

read.title: Designing a republic
text: The Declaration of Independence of 1776 claimed that governments get their power from the consent of the governed. Turning that idea into a working government proved hard. Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could not tax, regulate trade or raise an army on its own. When indebted farmers in Massachusetts rose up in Shays' Rebellion, many leaders concluded that a stronger national government was needed.

In 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia. They divided power among three branches so each could check the others, and between the national and state governments. The Great Compromise balanced large and small states by basing the House on population and giving every state two senators. Delegates also bargained over slavery, counting three-fifths of enslaved people for representation. Supporters wrote the Federalist Papers to win ratification, and opponents secured a promise of the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791.

Under the new government the nation grew quickly. The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled its size, and war with Mexico in the 1840s added the Southwest and California. Expansion came at a heavy price for Native nations forced west. It also reopened the most divisive question of all: whether slavery would spread into the new lands.
